overview.text: Dark matter is the name for unseen matter inferred from its gravitational effects; scientists have not directly identified what it is. Unlike ordinary matter, it emits, absorbs, or reflects little to no electromagnetic radiation, but its mass affects how stars and galaxies move. Astronomers infer its presence from galaxy rotation speeds that visible matter alone cannot explain and from gravitational lensing, in which gravity bends light from more distant objects. Evidence accumulated after Fritz Zwicky’s 1933 study of the Coma Cluster and Vera Rubin’s later measurements of spiral galaxies. Dark matter is thought to help shape galaxies and larger cosmic structures. Its composition remains unknown, and it is distinct from dark energy.

key_facts.text: Dark matter is inferred from gravity rather than seen directly; it does not emit, absorb, or reflect light in the way ordinary matter does.
Stars far from the centers of spiral galaxies move faster than estimates based on visible matter alone would predict, providing evidence for additional unseen mass.
Gravitational lensing—distortion of background light by gravity—lets astronomers map mass in galaxies and clusters, including matter they cannot see.
Fritz Zwicky proposed unseen matter to explain the Coma Cluster’s motions in 1933; Vera Rubin’s later studies of spiral galaxies added strong evidence.
Dark matter and dark energy are different: dark matter’s gravity helps bind structures, while dark energy is associated with the universe’s accelerating expansion.
